title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
summary: Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress urges staff forward and offers pay raises after Jensen Huang exit.
body: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high. Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday. Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject. The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up." Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands. Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

title: Fed officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI impact on inflation, minutes show
summary: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday released minutes from its October policy meeting at which it voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%.
body: Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk." More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December. The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective." In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December. Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability. Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint." "Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms." Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off. Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal." Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target. The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach. However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act. At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

title: Nvidia reverses, metals crash ahead of Anthropic IPO: Options Action Live
summary: Big moves have options traders wondering if Anthropic's IPO is spurring a rotation trade.
body: Is this what it takes to clear room for $1.5 trillion of new supply? Slumping crypto prices, a big Nvidia reversal despite good earnings, and now a sharp drop-off in metals prices from gold to copper — cross-asset selling has traders wondering if Anthropic's incoming IPO is spurring a rotation trade with the aim of freeing up cash to buy stock in the AI giant when it goes public on Thursday. Shares of Nvidia swung from $164 overnight to below $152 during Wednesday's trading session despite smashing analysts' expectations on revenue and guidance. Options volume on the stock was almost three times the average and showed a bullish bias despite the reversal, with almost twice as many calls trading versus puts, Cboe LiveVol data show. Meanwhile, metals prices fell across the board, led by a 5% sell-off in copper futures to the lowest since April. Gold futures lost more than 3% to $3,744, the lowest since September 2025, despite Treasury yields slipping on the session. Almost 300,000 options traded on the SPDR GLD Shares ETF (GLD) , with a slight bias towards calls. The catch for gold bugs is that more calls looked like they were initiated by sellers, according to Cboe LiveVol data, which show 52,000 calls sold on the bid versus 45,000 calls bought on the ask.

title: Read Jim Cramer’s full interview with Nvidia’s Colette Kress: Demand, buybacks and China
summary: Interim CEO Kress sat down with CNBC’s Jim Cramer Tuesday evening shortly after the AI chip giant delivered a quarterly beat and strong guidance.
body: Nvidia delivered another beat-and-raise quarter on Tuesday in the chipmaker's first report since Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as CEO last week amid a widening affair scandal. Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, exceeding estimates by nearly $7 billion, while earnings topped expectations by 20 cents per share. An excellent quarter by almost any measure. But investors remain skeptical about Nvidia's future without Huang, who famously founded the company at a San Jose Denny's in 1993. Shares fell 2.5% Wednesday, despite opening higher on the session. Will the company lose its smartest executives and engineers? Would Nvidia remain banker to the increasingly shaky neoclouds? Can it stay ahead of the competition? On Tuesday night, Colette Kress sat down with CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after delivering her first earnings call as interim CEO to answer these pressing questions and more. Jim Cramer: After the bell, Nvidia reported earnings, and what a quarter it was. The stock jumped in after hours in response. This is the first time we are hearing from the company since its founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as CEO last week. So let's check in with Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and now its interim CEO. Ms. Kress, welcome to "Mad Money." Colette Kress: Thank you for having me, Jim. It's really great to see you. Cramer: Thank you, Colette. The most important thing I heard tonight was that you increased your revenue growth forecast for next year. Previously, you said you would grow 70%. Now you're saying 75%, off of a higher base. How are you able to do that? Kress: Thanks. Very, very important to understand how much our customers are interested in our compute infrastructure and how much they need the agentic solutions out there. So the most important thing that we have been seeing is just, again, a continuous growth in terms of the demand that's out there. But we also have been working in terms of our supply. So an increase in supply, working with all of our different suppliers, whether that be focusing in terms of what we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together. We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% year over year for fiscal year '28. Cramer: Now, a lot of people have been saying that there was one man at this company. I've talked with you. There are another 49,000. How is the team holding up? Are there people who are saying, "You know what, this is not the Nvidia I know, I don't want to be there?" Is there a brain drain, as some people have told me? Kress: Yeah, really great question. And remember, the company has been built on the perspective that employees see Nvidia as their life's work. And many of them have been here for decades, working with us from both a technology and a business-and-operations perspective. And now where we're standing is focusing on the business, focusing on getting all of that work done. And I had been working already with leadership. Leadership is supportive of everything we're doing and is standing up to help as we pull all employees and leaders together to move forward. But we have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy really the work here at Nvidia. Where are you on buybacks versus lending aggressive amounts of money to, say, neoclouds? Because I think that the buybacks are a lot better for shareholders. title: Is Apple the safe haven investors think it is? Here's a way to trade it with less risk
summary: Traders have flocked to Apple's perceived safety in the wake of Nvidia's scandal. It may not be so safe, says Mike Khouw
body: For months, Apple has been the undisputed haven of the technology sector. As the industry grappled with the brutal reality of Nvidia's post-Huang future, investors blindly rotated into Apple, comforting themselves with the narrative that the Cupertino giant was uniquely immune to speculative overspending on artificial intelligence. While peers bled capital into server farms and data centers. At almost 37x forward earnings estimates, the stock is now priced for perfection, fully valued at precisely the moment the rest of the market is beginning to see multiples contract aggressively. Investors tend to huddle in the shelter of perceived safe havens, but that perceived safety can crack quickly in an adverse news cycle, as Nvidia shareholders recently learned. We've recently witnessed a bizarre parade of catastrophic system failures: the massive Microsoft outage, the FAA grounding flights, and cascading disruptions across major banking networks. Through it all, Apple was immune. Until today, when a widespread outage struck, knocking out iCloud, Apple Pay, and core support systems. The official explanation? Yet another internal update gone wrong. It's undeniably odd how all these major tech infrastructure failures are being chalked up to routine upgrades, all clustering around the exact same narrow timeframe. Without venturing too far into the conspiratorial, the sheer coincidence of these cascading digital blackouts suggests more systemic fragility than we may have realized. That's one thing at less than 10x forward earnings, as Nvidia is, or even at a market multiple. But Apple is twice as expensive as the S&P. Technically, Apple is balancing on a knife's edge. Shares have been relentlessly hugging the upper end of several channel-based technical indicators, such as the Bollinger Band. Apple has been priced at a steep premium for being immune to what ails other struggling stocks, but is now demonstrating similar vulnerabilities. Investors should ask themselves: what's the upside? That Apple trades at more than 40x forward earnings? 45x? Even at that rich multiple, that would represent only 18-19% upside from here. If the market suddenly decided that Apple's premium to the market would be just 50%, instead of 100%, that would be less than 28x forward earnings, a nearly 27% haircut to the current share price. Despite the high multiple, options prices are low versus the market. Market implied volatility is well above average (around the 93rd percentile). Apple implied volatility is actually just below the 1-year average. The price of index options is in the 98th percentile relative to Apple options. Because the stock is nominally expensive (translation? The share price is high in dollar terms), buying outright naked puts is highly capital-intensive. This is exactly where a put spread makes sense. By buying an at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money put and simultaneously selling a lower-strike put, traders can dramatically reduce the upfront capital cost. More importantly, this structure blunts the negative impact of theta, or time decay, ensuring you don't bleed premium while waiting for the technical breakdown to materialize. Furthermore, taking advantage of the natural put skew—where further out-of-the-money puts trade at relatively higher implied volatility—lets you finance your bearish bet efficiently by selling that inflated premium. Apple's historic premium is built on a foundation of immunity to the chaos infecting the rest of the market. Today's outage proved the company may be more vulnerable than investors appreciate. body: A stable Aa1 outlook removes one source of headline risk for Treasuries, but the growth upgrade cuts the other way for bonds. Stronger-than-expected activity strengthens the hawkish case being made by Fed officials this week and supports pricing for a December hike, which should keep front-end yields and the dollar firm. That’s a headwind for gold, which has tended to fall as Fed hike expectations build. Moody’s flagged energy prices as a drag on growth, a reminder that oil is the swing factor: further strength in crude would hurt growth and keep inflation pressure alive at the same time. Moody’s says the US economy has outperformed, and it’s leaving the rating alone. But it expects the things that drove this year’s strength, cheap money aside, to fade as higher rates, costly energy and a maturing AI boom slow growth to about 2%. Moody’s Ratings said the US economy has performed better than it initially expected in 2026, and it kept the country’s Aa1 sovereign rating with a stable outlook in its regular review of US creditworthiness. The agency pointed to real GDP growth of 3.4% at an annualised pace in the third quarter and now expects growth of 2.3% for the full year, before a slowdown to around 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Artificial intelligence features on both sides of that outlook. Moody’s said heavy spending on AI infrastructure is propping up growth in the near term and could eventually deliver lasting productivity gains, although it stressed that the size of those gains is still uncertain. At the same time, it expects the AI investment cycle to normalise, which would remove some of the support that has driven this year’s outperformance. The agency listed two other headwinds alongside that: higher interest rates and energy prices that remain elevated. Both are live issues. Several Federal Reserve officials have argued this week for further tightening, and oil markets remain on edge over shipping risks in the Middle East. Against those pressures, Moody’s said the economy’s capacity for innovation, a dynamic private sector and deep capital markets should continue to support investment and productivity over time. The rating rationale leans heavily on institutional strengths. Moody’s cited the country’s very high creditworthiness, its resilience to shocks and the dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency. It also said it expects the US to maintain its long record of effective monetary policy led by an independent Federal Reserve. That point is more than a formality: Fed independence is one of the pillars the rating rests on, so any perceived erosion of it would sit squarely within what the agency is watching. For investors, the review offers reassurance without much drama. A stable outlook signals that Moody’s sees no near-term pressure for a change in either direction, and its growth forecasts broadly match the picture of an economy that is running hotter than expected but set to cool as rates bite and the AI spending surge matures. The bigger question for markets is whether that late-year strength keeps the Fed on its hiking path into December. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The Australian dollar goes into the release near 0.6715 (as I post at least), close to its weakest level since January, so the bar for a relief bounce is low. A solid headline gain plus a steady or lower jobless rate would likely bring back some pricing for a February hike and lift the Aussie off its lows. A rise in unemployment to 4.8% or higher would probably extend the slide and pull front-end yields lower as traders price a longer peak. The minutes flagged that oil costs tied to the Middle East conflict could add to inflation, which means a soft print alone may not close the door on further tightening while crude stays elevated. --- Australia’s jobs report should recover most of September’s part-time losses, but with a divided RBA board split over how close the economy is to a sharper downturn, the unemployment rate matters more than the headline gain. Australia’s October labour force report lands at 00:30 GMT on Thursday (7:30 pm US Eastern on Wednesday), and it arrives with more riding on it than a typical monthly print. Economists expect employment to have risen by around 25,000 after September’s surprise 39,300 fall, with the unemployment rate seen steady at 4.7%, a five-year high, and participation unchanged at 66.8%. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics last month showed the decline was driven almost entirely by a 73,700 slump in part-time roles, while full-time jobs actually rose by about 34,000. That split is the heart of the case for a rebound. CBA expects the part-time drop to reverse, arguing that large swings in part-time work have historically unwound the following month. Its own internal labour data point to October growth of around 18,000, which it describes as a touch below the pace needed to keep unemployment from rising. In other words, even a healthy-looking headline gain could leave the jobless rate drifting higher. The release follows two days of mixed signals for the Reserve Bank of Australia. Minutes published on Tuesday showed six of nine board members backed November’s 25 basis point hike to 4.85%, the fifth increase of 2026 and the highest cash rate since 2008, judging policy not yet clearly tight enough to contain upside inflation risks. The three dissenters warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn, pointing to the delayed effect of earlier hikes, a bigger-than-expected rise in unemployment and a softening housing market. Wednesday then brought September quarter wages up 1.1%, the largest quarterly gain since late 2023, lifting annual growth to 3.5%, although real wages have now gone backwards for four straight quarters with inflation above 4%. The data matter because they speak directly to that split. A jobless rate stuck at 4.7%, or lower, would support the majority view that the labour market is loosening only gradually, which Westpac also expects as jobs growth runs below population growth. A rise to 4.8% or beyond would hand the dissenters fresh evidence and make it harder for the hawks to argue for a sixth hike. Several high-profile layoff announcements, including job cuts at NAB, Qantas, Rio Tinto and David Jones, add to the sense of downside risk, though economists note the numbers remain small relative to average monthly hiring. The RBA’s own forecasts already assume unemployment climbs, reaching 4.9% by the end of this year and a bit above 5% by late 2028, so a modest uptick would not be a shock. The bigger question is the pace. Traders have largely abandoned bets on a December move, and CBA judges the 7 to 8 December meeting will not be live, flagging February as the next realistic window for another hike. summary: Crude oil production in the most prolific basin in the United States has remained moderate despite the war premium that pushed prices to over $100 a barrel. For some, however, the very fact of production growth in the Permian is a surprise. The Permian has been the engine driving U.S. crude oil output growth for over a decade. Since then, shale production growth and Permian…
body: Thiel Doubles Down on Vaca Muerta as Trump Calls Venezuela an “Acquisition” What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Crude oil production in the most prolific basin in the United States has remained moderate despite the war premium that pushed prices to over $100 a barrel. For some, however, the very fact of production growth in the Permian is a surprise. The Permian has been the engine driving U.S. crude oil output growth for over a decade. Annual growth in the past consistently exceeded 1 million barrels--until 2020, when pandemic lockdowns killed demand and plunged U.S. crude into negative territory briefly. Since then, shale production growth and Permian production growth specifically have moderated. The basin spanning Texas and New Mexico still accounts for about 45% of the U.S. national total in crude and is the biggest contributor to total production growth. Yet even the war premium on prices this year has not been enough to convince shale drillers to drill, baby, drill. Enverus expects the country’s total crude oil production to rise by 378,000 barrels daily, with most of that coming from the Permian. The number is not particularly impressive compared to previous annual output jumps that were in the six figures but, Bloomberg noted in a report on the forecast, this would represent an annual increase of 2.8%, versus a much smaller annual production increase of 1.6% for 2025 versus 2024. The war premium, in other words, may have motivated Permian operators to ramp up drilling. “There’s a ton of operators that are just adding a little bit — which then on aggregate makes a big change,” Enverus analyst Stephen Sagriff told the publication. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates According to the Energy Information Administration , crude oil production in the Permian averaged 6.84 million barrels daily in the third quarter of the year, a modest increase on the second quarter when the Permian produced 6.82 million barrels daily. For the current quarter, the EIA expects Permian operators to ramp up further to 6.91 million barrels daily. The forecast for 2027 is also for slow, moderate growth that would bring the Permian’s total to over 7 million barrels daily. That would be up from just 2.2 million barrels daily back in 2017. Some have warned for years that oil production in the Permian cannot continue to rise as fast as it did five years ago, not least because such fast growth comes with a price tag, and that price tag consists of higher costs as horizontal wells become longer and longer, and greater demand for fracking fluid--which then goes back into the ground and eventually creates a problem. Reports that the Permian has a wastewater problem with storage capacity running out emerged last year, indicating that production growth may remain moderate and possibly even slow down further as regulators limit new wastewater disposal licenses in response to the problem. The above confirms that no basin, conventional or otherwise, can sustain the Permian’s early years rate of production growth. This is true especially about shale oil basins where wells get drilled and put into production faster but also deplete faster--and produce inordinate amounts of wastewater, apparently. Yet others have argued that there is still plenty of oil in the Permian to continue supporting overall U.S. oil growth for years to come, possibly decades. For now, it seems the latter camp is right, despite the slower growth rate, which is quite a natural response to price movements in the past few years. The shale oil industry is doing what the rest of the oil industry is doing: making financial discipline its top priority rather than seeing just how much oil they can pump if they really put their minds--and money--to it, as shale drillers did back in the original boom days. body: Thiel Doubles Down on Vaca Muerta as Trump Calls Venezuela an “Acquisition” What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The AI boom and the hyperscalers’ need for round-the-clock clean energy for their data centers meet the next-generation geothermal energy technologies developed by a number of start-ups. In a world first, Google this week signed an agreement with Quaise Energy to use power from the superhot rocks in the Newberry Volcano in Oregon for its existing data center operations in The Dalles. Quaise Energy, which develops utility-scale superhot geothermal energy, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) under which Google will buy 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian, Quaise’s flagship project in Central Oregon, beginning in the early 2030s. Quaise Energy says this first-of-its-kind deal will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy. Traditional geothermal energy is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot-water reservoirs that rarely exceed 600 degrees F. But superhot rock is a kind of enhanced geothermal that digs miles into the Earth to reach temperatures of nearly 800 F. Once superhot temperatures are reached, cold water is injected to create steam, which powers turbines. Quaise Energy says superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates At Project Obsidian, the company expects to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, a technology that can plug into existing drilling rigs to economically reach superhot geothermal conditions. Millimeter wave drilling is the keystone of superhot geothermal, Quaise Energy says , noting it is the only way to access the resource at scale while reaching economic and power parity with fossil fuels. “Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power,” Quaise Energy’s CEO and president Carlos Araque said in a statement. For Google, the agreement is more than just another PPAs for clean energy as the tech giant built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles, Oregon, in 2006. Oregon’s Newberry is also the site of a superhot geothermal project under development by another start-up, Mazama Energy, which just this week announced a first-of-its-kind chilling technology to protect critical equipment in 645°F superhot rock while increasing drilling speed by 20%. These breakthroughs address key barriers to competitive geothermal power, Mazama Energy says. “We can now address geothermal economics from both directions: lowering the cost of drilling each well and accessing hotter rock that can deliver far more energy,” Mazama Energy’s chief executive officer Sriram Vasantharajan said. “That is how utility-scale geothermal can become a truly competitive source of firm power.” Mazama in September raised $135 million in new capital to accelerate superhot rock geothermal commercial development, with strategic investors Shell Ventures and ConocoPhillips alongside John Arnold’s Centaurus Capital, Doerr Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Gates Frontier. Recent breakthroughs and growing interest from AI hyperscalers could supercharge superhot rock geothermal development. The Clean Air Task Force estimates that just 1% of the superhot rock (SHR) geothermal potential in the United States could produce 4.3 terawatts (TW) of firm, flexible power. That’s nearly four times the current total installed electricity-generating capacity in the United States. body: Thiel Doubles Down on Vaca Muerta as Trump Calls Venezuela an “Acquisition” Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… The war in Iran is causing an enduring upset in global oil and gas markets with long-ranging consequences for the economy, the energy sector, and the climate. For many countries, this has resulted in skyrocketing energy prices and a rapid shift toward renewable energies in order to fill the import gap. For China, the global leader in clean energy supply chains by a massive margin, this has resulted in a windfall – and a drop in greenhouse gas emissions. China has led global clean energy development for years now, spending more than the rest of the world combined on solar, wind, batteries, and other vital clean energy components. China still consumes vast amounts of fossil fuels and remains the world’s largest consumer of coal, but the massive buildout of cleaner alternatives has resulted in plateaued greenhouse gas emissions in recent years. And now, thanks to the impacts of the war in Iran, those emissions have started to dip. In the third quarter of this year, China’s carbon dioxide emissions saw their biggest fall since the COVID pandemic, at a 3.1 percent decline between July and September . A major uptick in electric vehicle adoption drove much of this decline, as consumers reacted to skyrocketing oil prices by ditching conventional gas-burning engines. As a result, China’s oil consumption fell by 4 percent year-on-year. Coal consumption also fell this year, although China continues to build new coal-fired plants. Emissions from the dirtiest fossil fuel fell by 3 percent year-on-year across the country thanks to the rapid buildout of renewable energy resources and comparatively slow growth of energy demand. “China added enough wind, solar, and nuclear generation over the same period to power Germany and more than twice as much as needed to meet China’s growing demand,” reports Yale 360. “Emissions from the production of steel and concrete also fell amid the ongoing construction slowdown.” China’s huge clean energy push hasn’t just transformed its own energy sector – it’s catalyzing a clean energy shift around the world. Rich countries have continued a pivot toward clean energy as the latest oil and gas crisis has shown the vulnerabilities of relying on fossil fuel imports, while cash-poor developing economies are starting to adopt these technologies at a previously unseen pace. For these countries that suffer the most from energy market volatility, cheap Chinese solar panels and batteries present a critical lifeline . “Some countries are pulling off stunningly fast energy transitions, adding solar so rapidly, it’s become a major source of electricity over the course of years — not decades,” CNN wrote in a report earlier this year. Indeed, Pakistan has become the surprise poster child of solar-plus-battery system growth as residents install rooftop solar and batteries faster than any other market on Earth. And Pakistan is not alone – emerging economies including Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, Morocco, Kenya, and Namibia have all overtaken the United States – the world’s largest economy – in their clean energy transitions. Increasingly, clean energy represents energy security and affordability as much or more than it represents sustainability. “Wind and solar cannot be embargoed, blockaded, or shut off by a foreign power,” David Frykman, General Partner at Stockholm-based venture capital group Norrsken, wrote in an op-ed for Fortune earlier this year. “Every terawatt-hour of domestic renewable generation is a terawatt-hour that no adversary can weaponize.” Plus, solar and wind have simply become too cheap to fail , in large part thanks to China’s manufacturing bonanza. body: Thiel Doubles Down on Vaca Muerta as Trump Calls Venezuela an “Acquisition” What I Cover My focus spans the global energy landscape and the technologies reshaping it, specifically focusing on oil and gas, renewables, and tech-driven market… Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) beat Wall Street’s revenue forecast by about $6.7 billion on Tuesday night, and copper fell for a fifth straight session on Wednesday. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 3.6% at $12,763 a metric ton in early London trading, according to Investing.com . Bloomberg had earlier reported a low of $13,019, the weakest since June 24, with the metal on course for its longest streak of weekly declines in two years. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in fiscal third-quarter revenue against the $109.1 billion analysts expected, according to LSEG data cited by Fox Business , and guided fiscal fourth-quarter sales to about $130 billion. It was the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and Saxo Bank said the board does not intend to bring him back. Tuesday’s tech rout pushed U.S. stocks to a fourth straight loss and Europe to its worst day since March, Saxo said. ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey said the AI selloff has raised concerns about copper “given the metal’s growing exposure to investment in power grids and data centres.” The dollar sits near a 19-month high, Reuters reported, and traders are waiting on the Federal Reserve’s October meeting minutes with more aggressive tightening already expected, Bloomberg said. TD Securities analysts added that U.S. tariffs on refined copper now look less likely, removing another source of support. The same rate worries pushed gold to a 14-month low near $3,780 an ounce, Saxo said. The slide predates Huang’s exit, and it has left copper about 14% below its $14,875 record from September . Goldman Sachs has called it a matter of positioning in AI-linked stocks, not a sign that fundamentals have loosened, as Oilprice.com reported last week . UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri said Nvidia has become a key source of funding for neoclouds and AI developers, and he expects it to pause those deals even if a new CEO holds the same course. A pause would push data center construction, and the copper that goes into it, further out. Aluminum was down 0.9% at $2,907.50 a metric ton by early afternoon in Shanghai, Bloomberg said, a day after the metal touched its lowest in almost a year. That came even though the premium of the LME cash contract over the three-month contract hit its highest since 1988 on Monday on thin stocks before easing, Reuters reported Tuesday. Manthey said she expects “this tightness to continue supporting prices in the near term,” though stronger production growth should gradually improve availability further out. Zinc lost 1% and tin 2% on the LME, Reuters reported, and nickel gave back part of Tuesday’s jump above its 200-day moving average. Chinese buyers, though, are paying a record premium to import copper, with the premium up 21% on Tuesday alone as inventories in the world’s top consumer run low. London is selling the same metal at its lowest price in nearly five months. title: AngloGold outlines $2.5B Quebradona copper plan
summary: The underground project, about 60 km southwest of Medellín, could produce about 80,000 tonnes of copper a year.
body: AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU; JSE: ANG) plans to spend $2.5 billion to build its Quebradona copper project in Colombia if it secures an environmental licence that has eluded the company since its first application in 2019. The underground project, about 60 km southwest of Antioquia’s capital, Medellín, could produce about 80,000 tonnes of copper a year and generate about $1.5 billion in annual exports, AngloGold said Tuesday at an investment event in New York. “We are confident that, once the environmental approvals are obtained, the project will move towards the start of construction in 2028,” Colombian Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo said in a statement issued in Spanish by AngloGold’s local unit. That timetable hinges in part on a 2025 order that created a temporary protected area covering the project and bars new environmental licences for mining in the zone while it’s in force. The restriction is due to run into mid-2028. AngloGold challenged the order in court and wrote down $98 million in project costs that year. AngloGold shares fell 7.9% to $78.01 Wednesday afternoon in New York amid global declines in mining and metals stocks. That valued the company at about $39.5 billion. AngloGold CEO Alberto Calderón told Colombia’s Blu Radio on Wednesday that he expects the licensing process to take 12 to 18 months. AngloGold could spend about $2 billion in the first two years of construction if it secures the licence, he said. Colombia’s environmental licensing agency shelved the application in 2021 after identifying gaps in the company’s studies, including on groundwater, tailings storage and potential ground subsidence. The National Mining Agency in August extended exploration to December 2027, giving AngloGold time to complete more geological, environmental and water studies. The company has begun consulting communities for a new environmental impact study. Quebradona hosts 120 million probable tonnes grading 1.23% copper for 1.47 million tonnes of contained metal, according to AngloGold’s year-end 2025 estimate. The planned plant would produce a copper concentrate with gold and silver as byproducts. title: Collective hits gold in rock classed as waste at Apollo
summary: Collective discovered gold and silver in waste rock at its Apollo deposit in Colombia, planning to invest $100M next year.
body: Collective Mining (TSX, Nasdaq: CNL) has found gold and silver in rock counted as waste inside the proposed pit at its Apollo deposit in Colombia, a day after outlining plans to spend $100 million (C$143 million) in the country next year. Of 17 holes in the shallow halo around Apollo, 15 cut intervals above the open-pit cut-off grade. All 10 holes from one drill pad hit gold and silver near surface. One cut 107.85 metres at 0.79 g/t gold and 14 g/t silver from 3.75 metres depth. A hole drilled from another pad cut 146.1 metres at 0.66 g/t gold, 19 g/t silver and 0.04% copper from 106.5 metres depth, extending below the pit floor and up to 60 metres beyond the resource boundary, Collective said Wednesday . “Overall, results suggest the pit shell understates the [shallow halo zone],” National Bank of Canada Capital Markets mining analyst Don DeMarco wrote Wednesday. Turning some of the rock already slated for removal into mill feed “could ultimately improve open-pit economics,” he said. Drilling has tested about 45% of the halo, up from 41% at the previous update, DeMarco estimated. The latest results are lower grade but cover longer intervals. Across 28 intervals in 15 holes, he calculated an average of 0.83 g/t gold-equivalent over 42.4 metres, compared with 1.18 g/t over 19.3 metres in the previous batch. Apollo is part of the Guayabales project about 80 km south of Medellín. Collective plans to test extensions beyond the pit next year, update the resource in late 2027 or early 2028 and complete its first preliminary economic assessment shortly afterwards. Next year’s spending would fund exploration and move Guayabales through licensing, executive chairman Ari Sussman said at a Colombian government event in New York on Tuesday. Collective aims to submit Apollo’s environmental licence application in the second half of 2027. Up to a further $1 billion in investment through 2030 depends on obtaining the licence, Colombian Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo said. Permits also stand between AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) and a much larger copper investment in neighbouring Antioquia. Its proposed Quebradona project would cost about $2.5 billion and could produce 80,000 tonnes of copper a year, corporate affairs executive Stewart Bailey said at the event. Restrepo said construction could start in 2028 if approvals come through. Collective shares dropped 7% to C$15.62 Wednesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$1.5 billion. The stock has fluctuated between C$13.81 and C$30.12 in the past year. Miners like Aclara are awaiting greater clarity over how Brazil’s new framework, approved in September, will work in practice.

title: Phoenix hits broad gold and copper at old BC mine
summary: The company hit broad intervals of copper and gold at Lexington in southern British Columbia.
body: Phoenix Metals (TSX: PCA) hit broad intervals of copper and gold at Lexington in southern British Columbia, where it is testing whether an old underground mining district could support an open pit. Hole LXDDH-26-001 cut 169 metres grading 1.02 grams gold, 0.22% copper and 3.79 grams silver from 41 metres depth, Phoenix said Wednesday in a statement. A second hole cut 233.5 metres at 0.26 grams gold, 0.14% copper and 0.86 grams silver from 8.5 metres depth. The company has yet to establish true widths. “These holes demonstrate the potential for Lexington to be developed into a bulk tonnage open pit target,” CEO Nick Campbell said in the release. Hole LXDDH-26-001 “demonstrates how the high-grade structures within the broad mineralized zone at Lexington can potentially upgrade gold values within a bulk tonnage target,” Miners at Lexington and the nearby City of Paris workings followed narrow, high-grade structures underground. Phoenix drilled through the surrounding rock to see how much lower-grade material might be mined alongside those structures. Its strongest hole included a higher-grade 38-metre interval. The first batch also shows how much the gold content varies across the target, with two other holes averaging 0.18 and 0.20 g/t gold over more than 180 metres each. Phoenix has traced a target over 1.5 km along strike and about 300 metres across using its drilling, surface mapping and more than 170 historical holes. That footprint is an exploration target. Testing whether it can support an open pit will require a resource estimate and an economic study. Phoenix completed 20 Lexington holes totalling 6,350 metres through October. The company expects more Lexington assays and the first results from nearby Phoenix South in December. Shares of Phoenix dropped 20% to 85¢ Wednesday morning in Toronto for a market value of about $77 million (US$54 million). The stock is at its lowest level since the company went public in July. title: Oil falls on Nov 18 as US crude stocks rise by 3.4m barrels - Nation Thailand
body: US crude fell to its lowest close since August 26 on November 18, 2026, after a larger-than-expected rise in US crude and fuel stocks strengthened expectations that global oil supply would exceed demand. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell US$2.75, or 3.2%, to US$83.26 a barrel. Brent crude fell US$1.19, or 1.28%, to US$91.95. Both benchmarks recovered some ground before the close. WTI had been down more than US$4 a barrel during the session, while Brent had fallen by more than US$2. The war in Iran and the threat to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz helped limit the declines. US commercial crude stocks reached 417.8 million barrels in the week ending November 13, according to the US Energy Information Administration. The weekly rise of 3.4 million barrels far exceeded the 58,000 barrels forecast by analysts in a Reuters poll. US petrol stocks rose by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million, more than three times the expected increase of 1.6 million barrels. Distillate stocks, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million, against a forecast rise of 1.3 million. Analysts at Gelber & Associates said the inventory figures prompted fresh selling. Attacks on commercial shipping still threatened oil deliveries through Hormuz, they said, but those risks had “provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus”. The price gap between Brent and WTI reached its widest in about two weeks on November 17, according to London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) data. US crude then fell more sharply than Brent on November 18. Both benchmarks were on course to lose about 20% in November as Middle Eastern exports rose and shipping rates fell sharply. June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, said it had become uneconomic to ship WTI to Asia and north-west Europe. A further fall in the US price relative to Brent could make those sales profitable again. Goh said rising crude stocks on the US Gulf Coast were also widening the price gap. Both oil benchmarks had risen on November 17 as attacks on ships in the Middle East intensified, even as Iran continued talks with mediators from Oman and Qatar. LSEG analysts said that day that alternative routes could help regional supplies recover, but vessel movements showed that oil shipments through Hormuz were still unable to return to normal. ADNOC Logistics & Services of the United Arab Emirates said on November 18 that one crew member was missing and 11 were injured after an attack on one of its vessels in the strait the previous evening. In a separate incident on November 16, the crew of a liquefied petroleum gas tanker evacuated after a projectile hit the ship off Oman. Iran said it attacked US drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. It was Iran’s first reported attack on Kuwait, a US ally, since September. Bahrain, where the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet is based, said it had intercepted Iranian attacks. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on November 17 that they had launched five drones towards two pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which carries oil along a route that bypasses Hormuz. Two Western officials briefed by Saudi officials said Saudi Arabia was preparing for the conflict with the Houthis to last well into 2027. US and Russian officials expected US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to meet separately in China on November 19, in addition to a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump’s envoys had stepped up efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, with European leaders also expected to take part in discussions on post-war security guarantees and economic recovery. title: Nvidia retreats, weighs on AI stocks as strong outlook fails to dispel Huang uncertainty - The Globe and Mail
body: Nvidia shares ( NVDA-Q ) dipped on Wednesday, with analysts more optimistic about future earnings while also more cautious about future stock gains following the AI chip giant’s blockbuster forecast and uncertainty caused by CEO Jensen Huang’s departure last week. Nvidia fell 2.8 per cent, increasing its loss to 36 per cent from its Oct. 6 record-high close, with much of that drop related to Huang’s resignation after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two with Nvidia employees. Following Nvidia’s strong report and outlook, the average analyst estimate for its adjusted net income in its next fiscal year has climbed to US$393-billion from US$380-billion before Tuesday’s late-day report, according to LSEG data. At the same time, the average analyst price target has dipped to US$251.74 from US$265.70 on Monday. The stock was last at US$152. The higher earnings estimates and lower price targets show analysts believe Nvidia’s business remains strong but are applying a more cautious valuation, reflecting risks around the CEO transition and AI spending. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 has shed around US$2-trillion in market value so far in November, as investors reassessed lofty AI valuations alongside concerns over China, data center spending and tighter regulation. “We believe yesterday’s results have stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff, but they have postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety,” said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint. The next test of the AI trade will come when Anthropic prices its initial public offering later on Wednesday, which could value the frontier lab at up to US$1.4-trillion. Also weighing on shares of Nvidia and other AI companies, the Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the chipmaker. The AI trade has also been tested since the Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins stoked fears of tougher regulation of data center buildouts, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq into correction territory earlier this month. Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones ruled out reinstating Huang despite his offer to return. Heidrick & Struggles is leading the search for a permanent CEO among both internal and external candidates. The stock might struggle to climb further until the company names a permanent CEO and the new leadership shows it can deliver planned products, HSBC analysts said. Interim CEO Colette Kress has said it was “business as usual,” citing customer and supplier support. Nvidia’s forecast offered evidence that the upheaval has not delayed its product roadmap or weakened demand. Nvidia’s fourth-quarter revenue forecast beat analysts’ estimates, while the company also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75 per cent, saying demand continued to exceed supply. Third-quarter revenue more than doubled to US$115.84-billion, marking a 17th consecutive estimate beat, according to LSEG data. Adjusted gross margin reached 74.9 per cent. Nvidia expects it to bottom between 71 per cent and 72 per cent this quarter as higher supply costs bite, before recovering to between 72 per cent and 73 per cent in fiscal 2028. “Strong earnings have bought management time,” Saxo strategist Charu Chanana said. China contributed US$2.4-billion in licensed Hopper data center sales during the quarter, but Nvidia assumed no such shipments in its current forecast and said it was no longer shipping those products to the country. Management said the outlook considered current U.S. export controls, although it was still studying parts of the new rules announced on Monday, while demand elsewhere was expected to absorb the loss of China sales. “Kress also provided confident answers around Commerce rules, citing that demand is far exceeding supply and that Nvidia is studying the rules around the chip delivery to other countries,” said Christopher Brown, vice president of investme

body: In the morning session of the New York stock market on the 18th, direction diverged between economically sensitive stocks and tech shares. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 369.50 points from the previous close at 50,389.92 as of 10:05 a.m., extending its decline, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite turned higher, gaining 138.77 points to 24,467.15. Note: Dow figure as of 10:05 a.m.; Nasdaq figure at the same time. On the 18th, major US retailers including Target and Lowe's reported earnings in succession. Caution over additional rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve also weighed on the market, with selling in defensive names such as healthcare and retail stocks leading the way from the opening bell. The Dow opened lower. Retail earnings were generally solid. Target's August–October 2026 quarter saw same-store sales rise 5.6% year-on-year (vs. market expectation of 3.61% growth), with earnings per share of $2.65 (vs. market expectation of $2.08, including a $0.50 tariff refund), and full-year EPS guidance of $10.65–$11.40. Lowe's also reported earnings that beat market expectations. On monetary policy, Fed Governor Waller said in a CNBC television interview on the 18th that he is "very concerned" about inflation moving in an undesirable direction. He also noted that price increases are "broadening" and indicated that "a more aggressive approach is needed" to achieve price stability. He said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) should raise rates by 0.5% at its December 8–9 meeting, and argued that even if the committee settles for 0.25%, it should clearly signal an additional hike in January. "We may need to surprise people," he said, also indicating that the three rate cuts implemented in 2025 need to be reversed. Markets have fully priced in a 0.25% hike in December, with additional hikes in January and 2027 also being anticipated. Growing expectations for a year-end rate hike are capping upside for the stock market. On the other hand, Nvidia's strong earnings provided support for the market. The company's August–October 2026 quarter results, announced on the 17th, showed revenue of $115.844 billion and net income of $65.287 billion, both record quarterly highs. For the November 2026–January 2027 quarter, the company also provided revenue guidance of around $130 billion, up 91% and above market expectations. Note: The Nov–Jan guidance includes one more week of business days than usual and does not factor in any China data center revenue. Gross margin guidance is 71.0–72.0%, expected to decline from 74.8% this quarter. Following the strong earnings and bullish guidance, the company's shares rose in after-hours trading. Concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI)-related companies eased, and buying flowed into AI and semiconductor-related names. That said, Nvidia's stock closed at $155.46 on the 17th, down about 17% year-to-date and roughly 35% below its October high of around $240. The lack of a permanent successor CEO and uncertainty surrounding its China business have weighed on the stock. In this earnings report, the company disclosed that it has halted shipments of its China-bound data center product "H200." August–October revenue from H200 in China was $2.4 billion, and the November–January guidance does not factor in any China data center revenue. Founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, and the board has denied he will return. This was the company's first earnings announcement since his resignation. body: Nvidia raised its sales forecast for its next fiscal year, and reported stronger-than-expected results in its most recent quarter, in a striking signal of business confidence by the AI chipmaker following the resignation of longtime CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang . “Our momentum is real,” interim CEO Colette Kress said on conference call with analysts on Tuesday, citing strong demand for the company’s products, Nvidia’s ongoing technological advances, and the commitment of its employees. Kress, Nvidia’s longtime finance chief, made her debut as interim CEO on Tuesday’s earnings call, flanked by newly appointed chair of the board Harvey Jones . The pair took pains to project a business-as-usual attitude—even using the phrase—while seeking to put Huang in the rear-view mirror . The board of directors “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the call, noting that the company has retained executive recruiting firm Hedrick & Struggles to search for a permanent CEO. The comments were a direct rebuttal to Huang, who is seeking to reclaim the CEO throne just days after resigning amid revelations of multiple affairs, one reportedly with a Nvidia employee who reported to him and another with a woman some believe may be a Chinese spy. Shares of Nvidia were up more than 5% in after hours trading on Tuesday. The company’s stock has plummeted more than 36% in the past month, shedding more than a trillion dollars in market value. Investors have been spooked by the loss of Nvidia’s longtime leader, Huang, as well as by general concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Kress doused both concerns at once on Tuesday by raising sales expectations for Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 year, which is roughly equivalent to the 2027 calendar year. “We had originally indicated that we would be at about 70% growth year-over-year, and now we are are increasing that to 75%” growth,” Kress said, citing improvements in supply and ongoing strength in demand. The guidance was particularly striking because Huang himself had delivered the 70% growth forecast three months ago, framing it as an usually far-reaching forecast that reflected the exceptional strength in the business. In raising the annual revenue forecast by the equivalent of $20 billion or more, Nvidia’s message seemed to be that Huang was not so essential after all. “We got this,” Kress said during the call. “The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him,” Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors on Tuesday. Revenue in three months ended October 25 totaled $115.8 billion, roughly twice the amount Nvidia generated in the year ago period, and above the $109 billion expected by analysts. Net income increased 105% to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per share. The world’s leading maker of AI chips said it expects revenue in the fourth quarter to come in at $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—besting the $125 billion expected by analysts at the low point and potentially exceeding the target by billions of dollars. Nvidia said it would file its official 10-Q report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in “the coming weeks,” rather than on the same day as its earnings announcement as it traditionally has done. body: Whale exchange deposits are the number to watch. A sustained slowdown would support the argument that sellers are exhausted, while continued net inflows leave any rally exposed to supply from large holders. Listed miners such as MARA and Riot remain a source of spot supply as long as they keep selling their bitcoin, which also clouds the outlook for miner equities. US spot bitcoin ETFs lost roughly $2.1 billion between late October and mid-November, so the long-term buying Maredia describes has yet to show up in fund flows. For wider risk sentiment, the AI rotation idea needs bitcoin to rise on days when AI stocks fall, not simply lag them. --- A bitcoin CEO says the sellers are done, but the largest wallets are still moving coins onto exchanges, so the recovery case rests on a turn in flows that the data has not yet shown. Lava founder and chief executive Shehzan Maredia believes bitcoin may be nearing a turning point as selling from miners and large holders fades, but on-chain data, which tracks coin movements recorded on the blockchain, suggests the biggest wallets are still adding to supply on exchanges. Speaking in an interview with Anthony Pompliano, reported by Benzinga, Maredia pointed to three developments he sees as supportive for bitcoin’s longer-term outlook. He argued that miners and whales, the term for holders of very large amounts of bitcoin, may have already done much of their selling, citing the market’s relatively contained response to a recent major exchange hack as evidence. He also said long-term holders have kept buying despite falling prices, and that stablecoin payments are introducing new users abroad to bitcoin as a savings asset. Stablecoins are tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar, often used for cross-border transfers. Maredia expects investors to rotate profits from AI holdings into bitcoin, particularly with equity valuations stretched. In his view, the Democratic election sweep could bring tighter regulatory pressure on AI, which could speed up that shift in capital. He played down the importance of the Clarity Act, US legislation aimed at setting out how crypto markets are regulated, arguing that adoption, network security and savings demand matter more for bitcoin than further market-structure rules. The flow data is harder to square with the idea that sellers are spent. Entities holding 1,000 BTC or more are sending roughly $55 million more bitcoin to exchanges each day than they withdraw. That matters because coins are usually moved onto an exchange to be sold, while withdrawals into private storage tend to signal an intention to hold. The pattern reverses earlier periods when withdrawals dominated. Separate data showed whales that had held coins for years locking in around $295 million in profits on 10 November, their largest profit-taking event of 2026, with bitcoin near $73,700 at the time. Supply from listed companies has also been heavy. Fourteen public companies have sold a combined total of about 108,000 BTC this year, worth around $8.1 billion, with miners prominent among the sellers. Maredia does not expect another tenfold rally within a year. He sees bitcoin maturing into an asset with steadier returns and lower volatility, with the halving, the roughly four-yearly cut in the new bitcoin awarded to miners, still relevant but investor demand and market structure playing a growing role. The next thing to watch is whether whale exchange deposits begin to slow. A sustained drop would lend weight to Maredia’s case that selling is exhausted, while continued net deposits would suggest large holders are still using rallies to sell. Readers can also track whether spot ETF flows turn positive and whether bitcoin holds up on days when AI stocks fall, which would be the first real evidence of the rotation he describes. body: Gold extends its sell-off to its lowest level in 14 months, losing more than 30% from the record highs reached in early 2026. The precious metal is down more than 2% today, falling towards $3,750 per ounce, as markets almost fully price in a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December. According to UBS analysts, the recent decline primarily reflects changes in investor positioning rather than a fundamental deterioration in gold's long-term outlook. The Swiss bank has lowered its end-2026 gold price forecast to $4,500 per ounce while maintaining its end-2027 target of $5,000. Gold has lost more than 30% from its peak: Rising US real bond yields, a stronger dollar and expectations of further Fed rate hikes are weighing on the entire precious metals market. UBS expects a recovery in 2027: The bank believes that sustained central bank demand remains an important source of support, although a meaningful price recovery may take time. Key price levels for gold: The $3,800 level has been breached today, increasing the risk of a decline towards $3,600–$3,500. A recovery above $4,000 could provide an initial signal of improving technical conditions. The biggest challenge facing the gold market is not a lack of geopolitical uncertainty or a collapse in physical demand, but the growing attractiveness of US Treasury bonds. The yield on 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) has risen to around 2.92%, while nominal 10-year Treasury yields remain above 5%. This means investors can earn an inflation-adjusted yield of nearly 3% annually on US government bonds, whereas gold generates neither interest nor dividends. This distinction is fundamental to portfolio allocation. Gold competes not only with equities and the US dollar but also with relatively safe, income-generating assets. The higher real interest rates rise, the greater the opportunity cost of holding bullion. In such an environment, even persistently elevated inflation may fail to support gold prices if real bond yields are rising simultaneously. The situation is further complicated by the Federal Reserve's increasingly hawkish stance. According to today's futures market pricing, the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December stands at approximately 95%, with the remaining 5% assigned to a 50-basis-point increase. Comments from Fed officials, including Alberto Musalem, have reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening. UBS analyst Joni Teves believes the latest decline primarily reflects investors reducing their positions rather than a fundamental shift in gold's long-term investment environment. A stronger dollar, rising bond yields and investors shifting their attention towards artificial intelligence and energy stocks have limited capital inflows into precious metals. Furthermore, during the recent sell-off in US technology stocks, gold may have been sold to raise liquidity and reduce overall portfolio risk. This is an important distinction: gold can decline during periods of heightened risk aversion when investors need cash to cover losses or meet margin requirements elsewhere. In the short term, its high liquidity can paradoxically work against its price. However, UBS believes long-term investors remain relatively resilient despite the correction, while gold ETF holdings show little evidence of widespread capitulation. The bank also highlights increased central bank buying activity during periods of falling prices. Current forecasts suggest that several major financial institutions still anticipate a significant recovery in gold prices in 2027: At approximately $3,750 per ounce, UBS's end-2027 forecast would imply potential upside of around 33%. However, this does not mean the correction is expected to end quickly. On the contrary, persistently high bond yields and a strong US dollar could continue to limit the scale of any recovery over the coming quarters. body: Oil prices fell on Wednesday after US crude and fuel inventories posted larger-than-expected rises, according to the Energy Information Administration, adding to expectations of a supply surplus. Brent crude futures lost 1.28% to settle at $91.95 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures settled down 3.2% at $83.26. U.S. crude inventories rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended November 13, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a rise of 58,000 barrels. U.S. gasoline stocks rose by ⁠5.2 million ‌barrels in the week to 215.9 million barrels, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations ⁠in a Reuters poll for a build of 1.6 million barrels. Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels in the week to 104.9 million barrels, versus expectations for a rise of 1.3 million barrels, the EIA data showed. Those stock increases renewed selling pressure, Gelber & Associates analysts said, adding: "Attacks involving Iran and commercial shipping still threaten deliveries through the ‌Strait of Hormuz, but those risks have provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus." Meanwhile, both Brent and U.S. crude futures contracts were on track for declines of about 20% this month on rising exports from the Middle East, as signaled ​by plummeting shipping rates. The Brent/WTI spread was trading at its widest in about two weeks on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with WTI logging steeper declines during trading on Wednesday. "WTI arbitrage trades have been shut to Asia and Northwest Europe, thus WTI correcting more than Brent is the expected price movement to allow the arbitrage window to open again," said June Goh at Sparta Commodities, adding that rising U.S. Gulf Coast ⁠crude stocks are further contributing to the widening spread. But the continuing U.S.-Iran conflict and the risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz curbed price declines. Iran said ‌it had attacked U.S. drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the U.S. struck Qeshm ‌Island in the Strait of Hormuz. It was Tehran's first attack on the U.S.-allied Gulf state since September. Bahrain, home of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted Iranian attacks. Both oil benchmarks had settled higher on Tuesday as attacks on ships in the Middle East intensified, even as talks continued between Iran and mediators from Oman and Qatar. ADNOC ⁠L&S of the United Arab Emirates said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and 11 injured after one of ⁠its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. An LPG tanker was also struck by a projectile off the ⁠coast of Oman on Monday, prompting its crew to evacuate the ship. "Although regional supply may continue to recover through alternative routes, the latest vessel data suggests that normalization of flows through Hormuz is still not possible under current conditions," LSEG analysts ​said on Tuesday. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday that they had launched five ‌drones toward two pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which has been used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia is preparing for the conflict with the Houthis to stretch well into next year, said two Western officials briefed on the plans by Saudi officials. Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday, in addition to the trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. and Russian officials said. Trump's envoys have intensified diplomatic efforts ​to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with discussions that are ‌also set to involve European leaders focused on post-war security guarantees and economic recovery planning.

That explains much of the gap between the two benchmarks this month. A move from premium to discount valuations would be a lasting headwind rather than a one-day shock, and it favours rotation into cheaper domestic sectors such as banks, which also benefit from higher BOJ rates. The yen’s weakness offers exporters some cushion. Chip names, though, are trading on AI sentiment and Nvidia’s governance story more than on currency moves. Japan’s AI chip stocks were priced as can’t-miss growth plays. With profits in question, regulation looming and Nvidia in turmoil, investors are starting to ask for a discount, and the most expensive names look most at risk. Japanese stocks that had commanded a premium for their exposure to artificial intelligence are now being viewed as too risky by some investors, with Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia adding to doubts about the sector’s outlook, according to market reports on Thursday. Since Huang’s resignation, shares of memory maker Kioxia Holdings and chip testing equipment maker Advantest have each fallen by more than 9%, more than three times the almost 3% decline in the broader TOPIX index over the same period. Analysts describe AI-linked stocks as facing a triple hit. The first is a worsening profit picture, as questions grow over whether heavy AI spending can deliver adequate returns. The second is the prospect of tighter regulation following the US midterm elections, which revealed a political backlash against the technology. The third is the market turbulence unleashed by the leadership crisis at Nvidia, the industry’s bellwether. The key shift, analysts say, is in how investors price the theme. For much of the AI boom, Japanese suppliers to the chip industry traded at a premium because of their place in the global supply chain. That willingness to pay up may now be turning into a demand for a discount, as investors weigh the risks rather than the growth story alone. Not all stocks are seen as equally exposed. Fund managers noted that some of the largest AI-related names still trade at premium valuations, leaving them vulnerable to further selling. By contrast, stocks that have already fallen sharply may be closer to finding a floor, offering potential opportunities for selective buyers. The reassessment comes at a sensitive time for Japanese equities. The Nikkei 225 has fallen around 7% this month, in large part on concern over whether global AI investment can keep growing at its recent pace, and the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise interest rates again in December. Strong quarterly results from Nvidia this week failed to stop its shares sliding to a 16-month low, a sign that investors are focusing on governance and valuation risks rather than near-term demand. Gold's bad year is getting worse. Why its price keeps falling
summary: Gold has fallen sharply from its January record as higher interest rates and a stronger dollar change the investment case for the precious metal.
body: Precious metals investors can be forgiven if they feel like the past year has given them whiplash. Following a torrid run, which saw the price of gold hit new records 53 times in 2025, gold hit a historic high of $5,589.38 an ounce on Jan. 28, only to take an almost equally historic nosedive. On Wednesday, gold fell below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025, roughly a third below its peak. A convergence of factors pushed gold to historic highs earlier this year, according to Suki Cooper, global head of commodities research at Standard Chartered, the London-based multinational bank. Now a different convergence is bringing the price down. Which role it plays depends on the factors dominating the market and the psyche of investors, and right now, it's the currency argument that is bringing the precious metal down. Cooper said gold's climb began with strong physical demand that started in 2022 and raised the floor under prices. A second phase followed as investors rethought gold's place in their portfolios. With the cost of holding a non-yielding asset falling, they started thinking about the metal for the longer term. That, Cooper said, marked a turnaround. Until early 2025, Cooper said, long-term investors, especially those in gold-backed exchange-traded funds, had been cutting their exposure, which effectively added supply to the market. Last year, that reversed: ETF holdings, led by the SPDR Gold Shares ( GLD ), rose by roughly 800 tons and helped absorb the market's excess supply. "There was a lot of one-way interest, a lot of appetite to buy but not to sell," Cooper said. With selling in the secondary market staying muted, prices kept rising. By the end of 2025, net ETF holdings had passed 4,000 tons. Globally, gold ETFs had their strongest year ever for inflows, $89 billion, led by North America, according to the World Gold Council, with assets more than doubling to $559 billion in total. A weaker dollar , lower bond yields and worries about global debt "set the foundation for gold to hit highs in 2026," Cooper said. Investors who had been under-exposed to the metal kept buying. Evan Mills, a financial advisor with Scholar Financial Advising, a fee-only firm in Winston-Salem, N.C., said the lower interest rates, expectations of further rate cuts and a weakening dollar, were all reasons for investors to favor gold. "It was a perfect spot to be in if you were an investor in gold and commodities as a whole," Mills said. And investors did extremely well, especially with lower interest rates. "Cash doesn't do well in that environment, so a lot of people looked toward other places to hold their cash and maintain purchasing power," Mills said. The speed of the rally made some investors uneasy, and there was growing talk that the Fed could tighten. Then, Cooper noted, the Middle East conflict broke out and gold changed roles. It stopped acting as a portfolio safe haven and became "a liquidity provider." Cooper explained that because it was liquid and easy to sell, investors sold it to raise cash, which set off the first correction. Since then, she said, markets have been pricing in what the Fed will do. "In 2026, the Fed has leaned more toward higher interest rates," Mills said. This week, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors member Christopher Waller said a 50-basis point rate hike may be necessary to "shock people." "There are higher Treasury yields and a strengthening dollar, so the opportunity cost of holding an asset that doesn't produce income is much higher," Mills said. Mills said that in the current situation, gold investors are missing out on an environment in which cash actually does well, with money market funds that can pay 4% to 5%. "Cash maintains purchasing power, and you don't need to put it in an illiquid asset or one where you're relying on another person to see the value," Mills said.
